summary: Defines a framework for specifying restrictions on RTP streams in SDP. It introduces a new attribute, "rid", that identifies streams in an RTP session and lets the payload format parameters of each be constrained. This is useful for things like simulcast. It is standards-track.

eli5.summary: When you send several versions of the same video, each needs a label and rules, like "small one" and "big one". This document defines the labels and a way to attach rules to each.

subtitle: An SDP attribute that labels each RTP stream and attaches codec-independent limits such as resolution and bitrate.

tldr.problem: RTP payload types are a small space, and features such as simulcast and layered codecs add more streams to a session, so payload types alone cannot say which stream has which limits.
tldr.mechanism: A new media-level SDP attribute, a=rid, gives each stream an identifier and a direction, and optionally lists payload types and restrictions such as max-width, max-fps and max-br. The same identifier is carried in the RtpStreamId RTCP SDES item so packets can be matched to their description.
tldr.outcome: Endpoints negotiate per-stream restrictions through normal offer/answer. Restrictions can only narrow what is already allowed, and peers that do not know a=rid simply ignore it.

facts.value: pt plus 8 others, listed in Table 1

today: RFC 8851 is a Proposed Standard published in January 2021. It updates RFC 4855 and has not been obsoleted or updated itself, according to the metadata for this entry.

sections.title: Why Payload Types Are Not Enough
sections.content:
In RTP, the payload type (PT) field maps a packet to its payload format and SDP media description, with SDP rtpmap and fmtp attributes describing the media. Modern applications use multiple RTP streams in one session, or many codecs, and run into limits: [RFC3550] gives the PT only 7 bits, static assignments and multiplexing with RTCP shrink the usable numbers further, codec-specific SDP constructs vary, and PTs get overloaded to identify individual streams.

This RFC defines a framework for restricting source RTP streams, with SDP attributes that restrict payload formats in a codec-agnostic way. It complements a=fmtp. The new a=rid (restriction identifier) attribute only further restricts the parameters already set for a payload format and never relaxes restrictions from other mechanisms. Streams are tied to their descriptions with the RTP Stream Identifier SDES item from RFC 8852.

Unknown a= lines are ignored under normal SDP rules, so older implementations stay compatible. Implementations must be ready for successful negotiations with peers that neither indicate nor honor the restrictions.
sections.eli5: There are not many name tags available for streams, so a new, bigger labeling system is added on top. Old devices just ignore the new labels.

sections.title: The a=rid Attribute
sections.content:
The attribute is a media-level SDP attribute. Roughly, its form is a=rid:<rid-id> <direction> [pt=<fmt-list>;]<restriction>=<value>.... The rid-id binds the restrictions to the stream whose RtpStreamId SDES item carries that value.

  • Implementations that use a=rid MUST support the RtpStreamId SDES item and MUST send it for all streams that have a=rid lines remaining after negotiation.
  • Redundancy streams (such as RTX or FEC) MUST be bound with the RepairedRtpStreamId SDES item where it applies, set to the RtpStreamId of the source stream. It does not apply to formats that associate streams through shared SSRCs.
  • The direction is send or recv, independent of sendonly, recvonly and similar attributes. Recv restrictions on a sendonly stream are valid and apply if the stream later changes.
  • The optional pt= lists payload types usable in the stream. Without it, any PT from the m= line may be used.

A media description MAY have zero or more a=rid lines, and a given rid-id MUST NOT repeat within one. The attribute may be used for any RTP-based media transport. All RID restrictions MUST be registered with IANA.
sections.eli5: Each line says: this stream is called such-and-such, it is for sending or receiving, and here are its limits. The same name is stamped on the actual video packets so everyone can match them up.

sections.title: The Defined Restrictions
sections.content:
The RFC defines an initial set of restrictions aimed at video in a codec-independent way. All are optional and subject to offer/answer negotiation:

  • max-width and max-height: spatial resolution in pixels, measured at zero degrees of rotation if orientation signaling is used.
  • max-fps: frame rate; consecutive frames SHOULD NOT be closer than 1/max-fps seconds.
  • max-fs: pixels per frame (width times height).
  • max-br: bits per second of the RTP payload only, measured over any one-second sliding window. Short excursions are allowed.
  • max-pps: pixel rate, handled like max-fps after converting with max-fps = max-pps / (width * height).
  • max-bpp: average bits per pixel, a floating point value from 0.0001 to 48.0 with at most four digits after the decimal point.
  • depend: a comma-separated list of rid-ids this stream depends on, allowed only within the same media section.

The RFC defines no restrictions for audio or other media types, but notes that other documents may register them. Future restrictions go in a new IANA registry named RID Attribute Parameters under the Specification Required policy, and every restriction must only narrow what is otherwise allowed.
sections.eli5: The rules are things like: no bigger than this picture size, no more than this many pictures per second, and no more than this much data per second.

sections.title: Offer and Answer Procedures
sections.content:
The offerer MAY add a=rid lines to a media description. For each it MUST choose a unique rid-id and a direction, MAY list allowed payload types (the order is a preference that overrides the m= line order), and picks zero or more restrictions. It may name a restriction without a value to let the answerer set it. If a codec needs an a=fmtp line without RID, the offer MUST still include it, so an answerer that ignores a=rid still gets a valid description.

An a=rid-aware answerer checks each line in order and discards a line that is malformed, has a duplicate rid-id (all duplicates are discarded), has no valid payload types left, has unsupported restrictions in a recv line, has a bad depend reference, or conflicts with every codec in use. It does not need to understand every restriction in a send line.

For the answer, the answerer reverses each direction (send becomes recv and the reverse), MUST NOT change the rid-id, MAY only make restriction values more restrictive, and MUST NOT add restrictions that were not in the offer. It may drop payload types from a pt list, but must not add a pt list that the offer lacked.

The offerer matches answer lines by rid-id and discards lines that add restrictions, loosen values, add or widen pt lists, or conflict with codec properties. It MUST be prepared to receive an unrestricted stream. Later offers MAY change the number of RIDs; changed RIDs SHOULD use new IDs and unchanged ones SHOULD reuse the old ID.

Declarative SDP is out of scope. The RFC does not define RID use there.
sections.eli5: One side proposes limits, and the other side can only make them stricter, never looser. If one side does not understand the idea, the call still works, just without the extra limits.

sections.title: Interaction with Codec Parameters
sections.content:
Other mechanisms already restrict streams, such as codec parameters in a=fmtp (for example H.264 max-fs from RFC 6184) and a=imageattr from RFC 6236. RID restrictions are meant to add to those, so the combined result should be non-empty. For example, max-width=320 on a PT that an image attribute says has a minimum width of 640 is nonsensical, and the recipient ignores the line. An answerer wanting something stricter than other parameters allow can only discard the a=rid line.

The RFC then illustrates, non-normatively, how VP8 (RFC 7741) and H.264 parameters map onto RID restrictions. In each case the sent stream conforms to the smaller of the two values, for example min(rid_max_fs, h264_MaxFs * 256), using 256 pixels per macroblock. Most other H.264 parameters have no codec-independent equivalent.

For redundancy formats such as RED (RFC 2198) that wrap redundancy inside the source stream, the pt= list says whether the redundancy format and the individual source payload types are allowed. Future payload format registrations that define matching parameters SHOULD name them like the RID restrictions.
sections.eli5: If two rule books disagree, the stricter one wins. If the rules cannot all be true at once, the new rule is thrown out.

sections.title: Worked SDP Examples
sections.content:
The first example is an eight-way video call to a mixer. The offerer sends one video stream and receives seven, using seven bundled video media sections on the same port. One send/recv pair covers the maximum resolution (max-width=1280;max-height=720;max-fps=30). Receive streams are offered at 720p for the active speaker, 360p for the prior two active speakers, and 180p for the others.

The second shows scalable layers for a selective forwarding unit (SFU). Scalable encodings have dependencies between layers, unlike independent simulcast streams, so one send line uses depend=0 to point at the base layer. The example pairs the RIDs with an a=simulcast line. Simulcast details are in RFC 8853.
sections.eli5: In a big group video call, you ask for a large picture of whoever is talking and small pictures of everyone else, which saves a lot of data.

sections.title: IANA Considerations
sections.content: The RFC registers rid (long form Restriction Identifier) as a media-level SDP attribute, with Multiplexing Category SPECIAL. It creates the RID Attribute Parameters registry, seeded with pt, max-width, max-height, max-fps, max-fs, max-br, max-pps, max-bpp and depend. The RFC also updates RFC 4855 with guidance on naming format parameters and relating them to RID restrictions.
sections.eli5: The new label is entered in the official list of SDP words, and a new list is started for future rules.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
As with most SDP parameters, without integrity protection an attacker could alter a=rid attributes and change the session in unwanted ways, such as making a sender send more data than the recipient wants. Because the attribute can only narrow what is otherwise allowed, a modified value cannot produce a stream with higher bandwidth than one sent to an implementation without this mechanism.

RID identifiers are expected to be opaque, so they should not hold information that would be sensitive if seen by third parties.
sections.eli5: Someone could tamper with the rules in transit, but since the rules only make things smaller, they cannot make the call use more data than it normally would.

left.title: Offer line
left.desc: A send line describes what the offerer will send.

right.title: Answer line
right.desc: The answerer reverses it to recv, keeping the rid-id.
